article.body:
The day of the rally arrived. Streaming live from TH HQ, I spoke to the 5,000-plus chayolim from across the globe. “Pesach is coming up! The Rebbe emphasizes the importance of every single Yid having Shmurah Matzah at the Seder. This is our call! I encourage you to find a sponsor for just one box of matzah, and hand it out in a shopping mall, street corner, or anywhere else you can. We can’t leave even one Yid without matzah this Pesach. Send us a report of what you did, and you may see yourself in the next Hachayol magazine! C’mon, chayolim! Get up and be the chayol you are meant to be. Let’s make the Rebbe proud, and bring Moshiach now!” Shortly after the rally, the TH inbox became flooded with messages. We received thousands of reports describing the tremendous hatzlacha that

chayolim had while completing their Mivtzah Matzah missions. The photos alone spoke volumes. Tzivos Hashem temporarily hired two additional staff members to process the incredible influx of information, record them properly, and organize the duch’s to the Rebbe. What a special gift for these days surrounding Yud-Alef Nissan! The reports continued to pour in even minutes before Pesach, and throughout the weeks following Yom Tov as well. Here’s one such letter: Dear Tzivos Hashem, My family and I live in West Rogers Park, Illinois, where my brothers and I attend Cheder Lubavitch (Base #613773). Our Rebbeim at Cheder always encourage us to do our mivtzah missions, and I usually do them—but with the feeling that the really important mivtzoyim are taken care of by the older bochurim, and there’s not much that we chayolim can do. However, after the last TH rally, I actually felt that I do have the power to make a big difference! I asked my uncle if he would sponsor a box. He agreed to sponsor two(!), and even drove me to the store to buy them. I zipped into the store, carefully picked out

zip-lock bags (to make sure the matzah would remain chametz-free), paid for it with my uncle’s cash, and made my way back to his car.

person after that was much easier, Baruch Hashem! I was there for just 30 minutes and had half a box left. I carefully placed my box on top of a bench and started preparing the next few pieces to hand out. The box was wide open, with big English letters that read “Matzah Shmurah” on its side. When I finished, I looked up to find a distinguished looking man standing to my left, watching the box and zip-lock bags with interest. “Excuse me?” he said, “May I ask what you’re holding?” “Oh, these?” I held up a packaged zip-lock bag. “They’re matzah for the Passover Seder. Are you Jewish?” “Actually, I’m not.” he answered. “I noticed that your box says matzah on it, but these don’t look anything like the matzah we order each year for the Jewish partners in our law firm.” “What kind does your law firm order?” I asked. “Oh, you know,” he answered with a matter-of-fact tone in his voice, “normal Passover matzah, the ones that come in a square box.” In a very respectful way, I explained, “Well sir, today, most of the matzos you see in the store— like the square ones that you usually order—are machine-made. However, these round Shmurah Matzos are hand-made, which is the way that the Jewish people made their very first matzos thousands of years ago. We even use the same recipe.” “And what’s the original recipe?” he asked. “Very simple,” I replied, “Flour and water. But the baking process is super strict.” “How so?” he asked. “‘Shmurah’ means supervised. The wheat used for Shmurah Matzah is supervised from the moment that it’s cut to make sure that there is absolutely no contact with water. Even when the

wheat kernels are separated from the stalks and ground into flour, again, they’re supervised. No water allowed. Finally, when making the dough—and this is the trickiest part!—from the second the flour touches water for the first time, there’s a time limit of 18 minutes from bowl to baked—like already out of the oven before the 18 minutes are up. Any more than that, and you’ll be stuck with defective matzah; crunchy, but useless by the Seder.” “Wow,” he said, “this sounds like the real stuff. Can you tell me where I can make a large order of these matzahs?” “Hmm...well, I can get you the number of the matzah bakery, and you can be in touch with them directly. My name is Shneur by the way,” I added, arm extended towards him. “Ed Jones,” he replied, as he received the hand shake warmly. “Please give me the bakery’s number. I will be in touch with them.” Yesterday, Mr. Jones called me to say that his 312 boxes of Shmurah Matzah arrived from New York, and all 312 Jewish workers at the law firm were given Shmura Matzah for the Seder. So I just wanted to let you know that because of the video you showed at the rally, over 300 people (and their families!) had Shmurah Matzos at their Pesach Seder. And one more chayol believes that kids do have the power to make a difference. Thanks for the inspiration. -Shneur B. Imagine thousands of such letters, and you’ve begun to get a picture of the Mivtzah Matzah response that came in. Absolutely incredible, right?! The night after Yud-Alef Nissan, just as my head hit the pillow, the doorbell rang a few times. Again, my parents didn’t answer. “Please don’t let this be another

bad dream!” I thought to myself as I walked downstairs. Deep breath. “Who is it?” I asked out loud, and then I whispered quietly to myself, “Please don’t say Rafi Adler. Please… don’t say Rafi Adler!” “Sruli, it’s me, Noam.” Yesssssss. This wasn’t a nightmare! It was what I’d been waiting for since the Kinus Hashluchim. I opened the door. With his light Russian-British accent, he said, “Sruli, I’m so sorry to ring your bell at this hour. It’s just that I’m leaving the country tomorrow, and I’d like to finish the discussion that we had begun at the last Kinus Hashluchim.” My mind immediately went to the pajamas I was wearing, and I silently wondered if he had ever had a meeting with someone in sleepwear before. Well, he didn’t seem perturbed, and there were important things to discuss. “Of course,” I replied, my heart still shaking. I wanted to sound as present as possible. “I’ve been eager to continue discussing the parade.” “Can my bodyguard come in with me?” he asked courteously. “Sure. Please come in.” Whoops. Sorry reader! Silly me, forgetting to include important details. Like Noam’s last name— Mikhailov. Yes, the billionaire.

Do you have a mivtzoim adventure to share? We want to hear

it! Send it to mivtzoyim@tzivoshashem.org and maybe

you’ll get published too, to inspire others- just like Sruli! 10 524 וַאָרְקִּי 11
